subject: Physics
scope_summary: Authored conceptual spine for Newton's first-law reasoning, zero-net-force force inventories, free-body-diagram body ownership, and observer-frame choice. No equations or new depiction kinds are asserted.

resources.title: Track A authored Newton/FBD conceptual constructions
resources.rights_status: Author-created project draft; no external curriculum or scientific-review authority claimed.
resources.selection_reason: Supplies the four conceptual rungs required before a free-body-diagram product can be authored, without creating a renderer or gate relation.

buckets.title: Newton's first law and free-body diagrams
buckets.badge_reason: The difficult work is separating motion from change of motion, then assigning each force to the body it actually acts on.

conventions.statement: Choose the body before listing forces; each listed force must name an external agent acting on that body.
State whether the observer is accelerating before deciding whether a pseudo-force is part of the chosen description.

scope.covers: Qualitative first-law reasoning, force cancellation, free-body-diagram ownership, and frame choice.
excluded: A canonical FREE_BODY_DIAGRAM representation or renderer implementation.

capabilities.action: Relate zero net force to unchanged velocity.
capabilities.success_criterion: Accept steady motion as compatible with zero net force.

capabilities.action: Distinguish zero net force from the absence of individual forces.
capabilities.success_criterion: Recognize that nonzero forces can cancel in the net force.

capabilities.action: Assign each force arrow to the body on which that force acts.
capabilities.success_criterion: Place a partner force on the other body's diagram rather than the chosen body's diagram.

capabilities.action: Decide whether an observer description requires a pseudo-force.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identify accelerating-observer cases that need the added pseudo-force convention.

microtopics.title: Zero net force allows steady motion
microtopics.badge_reason: Everyday friction makes continued motion look as if it needs a continuing push.
entry_assumptions: Can tell whether an object's velocity is changing.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Zero net force does not mean zero motion; it means velocity does not change, so rest and steady motion are both compatible with the same condition.

teaching_path.action: Separate the statement 'is moving' from the statement 'is changing its velocity.'
teaching_path.why_valid: Motion and change of motion are different observations, and only the second identifies acceleration.
teaching_path.output: state A: moving steadily.  state B: speeding up, slowing down, or turning.

teaching_path.action: Imagine a low-friction cart after the hand has stopped touching it and compare successive equal-time snapshots.
teaching_path.why_valid: Once the hand is gone, a continuing steady velocity can be observed without a continuing forward push.
teaching_path.output: successive equal-time snapshots -> equal forward position advances; velocity unchanged.

teaching_path.action: Compare the released moving cart with a cart that starts at rest under the same zero-net-force condition.
teaching_path.why_valid: If both keep their initial velocities, the rule is about unchanged velocity rather than about rest.
teaching_path.output: moving cart: stays steady.  resting cart: stays at rest.  both show no velocity change.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A force must keep acting in the direction of motion or the object must stop.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A low-friction cart is pushed and then released. After the hand loses contact, what horizontal force is required merely to keep it moving steadily?
misconceptions.repair: Separate velocity from change of velocity: a net force is required for acceleration, not for the existence of motion.

exit_task.prompt: One cart is at rest and another moves steadily in a straight line. For each, decide whether zero net force is compatible with the motion and explain the common rule.

answer.summary: Zero net force is compatible with both. Each cart can keep its current velocity unchanged.
reasoning: Rest is a zero velocity that stays zero.
Steady straight motion is a nonzero velocity that stays unchanged.
The shared condition is no change of velocity, not no motion.
answer.check: Ask whether the motion description contains speeding up, slowing down, or turning. If none occurs, zero net force remains compatible.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer classifies motion qualitatively and asserts no computed force or acceleration.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created first-law contrast. It states no force equation and promotes no candidate-packet formula.

predict.prompt: A low-friction cart is already moving when the push ends. Must a new forward force keep acting just to preserve that motion?
predict.defensible_answer: No. If the net force is zero, the cart can keep the velocity it already has.

attempt.produces: A two-case prediction for a released moving cart and an initially resting cart under the same zero-net-force condition.

rubric.criterion: The moving cart is allowed to continue steadily.
The resting cart is allowed to remain at rest under the same rule.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizing unchanged velocity as the common condition.

accepted: 'The moving cart keeps moving steadily; the resting cart stays at rest. Neither has to change velocity.'
rejected: 'Zero net force makes both carts stop.' This turns zero net force into a command for zero velocity rather than unchanged velocity.

route.ask: After the hand leaves the cart, is the hand still exerting the forward push?
route.why_this_ask: It removes the continuing-contact explanation before discussing what the cart does.

route.ask: What would count as a change of velocity in the next few moments?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must name acceleration-like changes rather than equate movement itself with force.

route.ask: If none of those changes occurs, what part of the cart's motion is staying the same?
route.why_this_ask: It identifies unchanged velocity as the invariant.

route.ask: Does that same rule also allow a cart whose starting velocity is zero?
route.why_this_ask: The rest case checks that the learner has not replaced one special state with another.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path presents the moving and resting cases as a finished comparison. The learner route first removes the push, defines what change would look like, then discovers that both cases share unchanged velocity.

boundary_test.prompt: A cart moving east begins to slow down. Can zero net force still describe that interval?
boundary_test.answer: No. Slowing down is a change of velocity, so the zero-net-force condition no longer fits the stated interval.
boundary_test.confirms: The rule is about unchanged velocity, not simply about whether the object is moving.

microtopics.title: Nonzero forces can cancel
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners often read a zero total as evidence that nothing is present instead of as cancellation among directed contributions.
entry_assumptions: Can interpret zero net force as unchanged velocity.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Several nonzero forces can act on one body while their directed sum is zero; the motion responds to the net result rather than to the mere presence of forces.

teaching_path.action: List two opposite pushes on the same object as separate contributions before combining them.
teaching_path.why_valid: Keeping the contributions visible prevents a zero total from being mistaken for no forces.
teaching_path.output: leftward push: present.  rightward push: present.

teaching_path.action: Make the two opposite pushes equal in size and combine their directional effects.
teaching_path.why_valid: Equal opposite contributions cancel in the net result while each contribution still exists.
teaching_path.output: two nonzero opposite pushes -> net force: zero.

teaching_path.action: Increase both opposite pushes together while keeping them equal.
teaching_path.why_valid: The individual forces change while the zero net result persists, directly separating the parts from their sum.
teaching_path.output: larger opposite pushes: still net force zero; individual forces remain nonzero.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If the net force is zero, no forces are acting.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A book rests on a table. Are there no forces on the book, or can nonzero forces add to zero?
misconceptions.repair: List every interaction force on the body, then combine their directions; cancellation belongs to the net result, not to the individual forces.

exit_task.prompt: An object has two equal opposite forces acting on it. Explain what is zero and what is not, then state what motion change the net result predicts.

answer.summary: The net force is zero, but both individual forces are nonzero. The zero net result predicts no change of velocity.
reasoning: Each force remains an actual interaction on the body.
Opposite equal directional effects cancel only when combined.
A zero net force is consistent with unchanged velocity.
answer.check: Increase both forces equally; the net remains zero even though neither individual force disappears.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The response uses only equality, opposition, and zero/nonzero classification; it asserts no computed force magnitude.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created cancellation contrast, deliberately separate from any force-acceleration equation.

predict.prompt: Two people push the same box equally hard in opposite directions. If the box has zero net force, does that mean neither person is exerting a force?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Both forces are present; their opposite directional effects cancel in the net result.

attempt.produces: A force inventory that keeps both opposite contributions visible plus a separate statement of the net result.

rubric.criterion: Only the combined result is labelled zero.
rubric.evidence_of: Locating the zero at the level of the sum.

accepted: 'Left push present; right push present; equal and opposite, so the net force is zero.'
rejected: 'No forces act because the net is zero.' This deletes the interactions instead of combining them.

route.ask: Before adding anything, how many pushes are physically acting on the box?
route.why_this_ask: It fixes the inventory before a zero total can erase it.

route.ask: Which directions do those pushes point?
route.why_this_ask: Cancellation requires direction, so the learner has to preserve it.

route.ask: If the two sizes match, what happens to the combined directional effect?
route.why_this_ask: The zero is derived from the pair rather than assumed from the motion.

route.ask: If both people push harder by the same amount, which statements change and which stay true?
route.why_this_ask: The variation separates individual magnitudes from the net result.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path lists and combines the forces. The learner route commits to the inventory first, then derives cancellation and tests it by changing both contributions together.

boundary_test.prompt: One of the two equal opposite pushes is removed. Is the net force still zero?
boundary_test.answer: No. One nonzero force remains without an equal opposite contribution to cancel it.
boundary_test.confirms: Zero net force came from cancellation between present forces, not from a property of the object.

microtopics.title: A free-body diagram belongs to one chosen body
microtopics.badge_reason: Equal-and-opposite partner forces look like natural cancellations until the learner asks which body each arrow actually acts on.
entry_assumptions: Can keep several forces visible even when their net effect is zero.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A free-body diagram contains forces acting on one chosen body only; the equal-and-opposite partner of an interaction acts on the other body and belongs on that other body's diagram.

teaching_path.action: Choose the cart as the body to describe and require every arrow to answer 'who acts on the cart?'
teaching_path.why_valid: The ownership question gives one mechanical test for whether a force belongs on the chosen body's diagram.
teaching_path.output: chosen body: cart.  every listed arrow must be an agent -> cart force.

teaching_path.action: For the horse-cart contact, place the horse-on-cart force on the cart diagram and place the cart-on-horse partner on a separate horse diagram.
teaching_path.why_valid: The two forces belong to one interaction but act on different bodies, so combining them on one body's diagram changes the question being asked.
teaching_path.output: cart diagram: horse -> cart.  horse diagram: cart -> horse.

teaching_path.action: Switch the chosen body from cart to horse and rebuild the inventory from the ownership question.
teaching_path.why_valid: A correct diagram changes when the chosen body changes even though the physical interaction is the same.
teaching_path.output: switch body -> switch which contact-force arrow belongs in the diagram; partner arrows never cancel on one diagram.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Equal and opposite partner forces cancel each other on one body's free-body diagram.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A horse pulls a cart and the cart pulls back equally. Which of those two forces acts on the cart, and which acts on the horse?
misconceptions.repair: Choose one body first. Put only forces acting on that body on its diagram; draw the partner force only when the other body is chosen.

exit_task.prompt: A person pushes a box. Describe the two contact-force partner arrows and state which one belongs on the box's free-body diagram.

answer.summary: The person's force on the box belongs on the box diagram. The box's equal-and-opposite force on the person belongs on the person's diagram.
reasoning: Ask which member of the contact pair acts on the box.
The partner acts on the person, so it cannot cancel the first force on the box diagram.
answer.check: Switch the chosen body to the person; the membership of the two partner arrows must switch with it.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer assigns force ownership qualitatively and contains no computed force value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created body-ownership construction. A drawable FREE_BODY_DIAGRAM representation is intentionally not authored in this track.

predict.prompt: A horse pulls a cart while the cart pulls back on the horse. If you draw only the cart, should both of those horizontal forces appear on the cart's free-body diagram?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Only the horse-on-cart force acts on the cart; the cart-on-horse partner belongs on the horse's diagram.

attempt.produces: Two separate body inventories, one for the cart and one for the horse, with the contact partner arrows assigned to the body each arrow acts on.

rubric.criterion: Each diagram contains only the member of the contact pair acting on its chosen body.
rubric.evidence_of: Using force ownership rather than visual cancellation.

rubric.criterion: The partner arrows are placed on different body diagrams.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizing that equal-and-opposite partners do not cancel within one body's inventory.

accepted: 'Cart: horse pushes cart forward. Horse: cart pushes horse backward.' The two arrows are on different diagrams.
rejected: Both equal-and-opposite arrows drawn on the cart and crossed out. This puts a force acting on the horse into the cart's inventory.

route.ask: Which single body are you describing first?
route.why_this_ask: The diagram has no ownership until a body is chosen.

route.ask: For the horse-on-cart force, which object receives the push?
route.why_this_ask: The receiver test decides membership without requiring a named law.

route.ask: For the cart-on-horse partner, which object receives that push?
route.why_this_ask: The same test places the partner on the other diagram.

route.ask: When you switch the chosen body, which contact arrow moves into the new inventory?
route.why_this_ask: Rebuilding the diagram tests whether body ownership, rather than arrow pairing, controls placement.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path demonstrates two correct diagrams. The learner route begins from one chosen body and repeatedly applies the receiver test until the separation of partner arrows is forced.

boundary_test.prompt: Two hands push the same box equally in opposite directions. Can those two forces both appear on the box's free-body diagram?
boundary_test.answer: Yes. Both hands act on the same chosen box, so both forces belong there and may cancel in the net force.
boundary_test.confirms: The rule is body ownership, not a ban on opposite arrows appearing together.

microtopics.title: An accelerating observer needs a declared pseudo-force convention
microtopics.badge_reason: The same physical interactions can be described by observers with different accelerations, and the extra convention is easy to omit when the observer is inside the accelerating vehicle.
entry_assumptions: Can build a force inventory for one chosen body.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A force-based account depends on the observer: a non-accelerating observer uses the physical interaction forces, while an accelerating observer must add the corresponding pseudo-force convention to describe the same observed motion consistently.

teaching_path.action: Describe the same loose object first from the roadside and then from inside a bus, stating whether each observer is accelerating.
teaching_path.why_valid: The observer choice is part of the model; leaving it implicit makes two different descriptions look contradictory.
teaching_path.output: roadside: observer acceleration zero.  bus during start: observer acceleration forward.

teaching_path.action: Keep the physical interactions unchanged and compare what the accelerating bus observer sees the loose object do relative to the bus.
teaching_path.why_valid: The apparent backward motion comes from the observer's changing motion, not from a newly discovered physical contact on the object.
teaching_path.output: bus accelerates forward -> loose object appears to shift backward relative to the bus.

teaching_path.action: Add a backward pseudo-force only in the accelerating-observer description and compare it with the roadside account.
teaching_path.why_valid: The added convention compensates for the observer's acceleration without inventing a new physical interaction.
teaching_path.output: roadside account: physical forces only.  accelerating-bus account: same physical forces plus backward pseudo-force.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The same ordinary-force diagram can be used unchanged in any accelerating observer's frame.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A loose mass appears to accelerate backward inside a bus that starts forward. Can the bus observer use only the same physical-force inventory as the roadside observer?
misconceptions.repair: State the observer first. Use physical interactions alone for a non-accelerating observer; for an accelerating observer include the corresponding pseudo-force consistently.

exit_task.prompt: A bus accelerates forward and a loose object appears to move backward relative to the bus. Compare the roadside and bus-observer force descriptions without calculating any magnitude.

answer.summary: The roadside description uses the physical interactions only. The accelerating bus description adds a backward pseudo-force convention to account for the observer's acceleration.
reasoning: The physical interactions on the object do not change merely because the observer changes.
The bus observer is accelerating relative to the roadside observer.
The pseudo-force belongs to that accelerating-observer description rather than to a new physical agent.
answer.check: Repeat the comparison once the bus moves at steady speed; the extra pseudo-force should no longer be needed for the observer change alone.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer classifies observer descriptions and contains no computed pseudo-force or acceleration magnitude.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created observer-choice boundary. No pseudo-force equation is asserted; a quantitative treatment would require upstream gate ownership.

predict.prompt: A bus starts forward and a loose object seems to shift backward to a passenger. Before adding any new force, did a new physical agent suddenly begin pulling the object backward?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The physical interactions need not change; the passenger's observer description changes because the bus is accelerating.

attempt.produces: Two labelled observer descriptions of the same object: roadside and accelerating bus, with a statement of where the pseudo-force convention appears.

rubric.criterion: The roadside description keeps only physical interactions.
rubric.evidence_of: Not inventing a new physical agent when the observer changes.

rubric.criterion: The bus description adds the pseudo-force specifically because that observer accelerates.
rubric.evidence_of: Attaching the convention to observer acceleration rather than to the object.

accepted: 'Roadside: physical forces only. Accelerating bus: same physical forces plus a backward pseudo-force for the bus description.'
rejected: 'A new backward physical force appears when the bus starts.' This confuses an observer convention with an interaction.

route.ask: Did the set of physical objects touching or attracting the loose object change when the bus started?
route.why_this_ask: It tests whether a new physical agent exists before any observer convention is introduced.

route.ask: Which observer is accelerating during the bus start?
route.why_this_ask: The extra convention is tied to observer acceleration, so this must be explicit.

route.ask: What does the passenger see the loose object do relative to the bus?
route.why_this_ask: The observed relative motion is the phenomenon the bus description has to account for.

route.ask: Where should the pseudo-force be added so the two descriptions remain consistent about the same physical situation?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must attach the added term to the accelerating observer rather than to a new physical interaction.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path compares two observer accounts directly. The learner route first rules out a new physical agent, identifies which observer accelerates, then introduces the pseudo-force as a modelling convention.

boundary_test.prompt: The bus now travels at constant velocity. Does changing from the roadside observer to the bus observer by itself require the added pseudo-force?
boundary_test.answer: No. With no observer acceleration in this comparison, the extra pseudo-force convention is not required merely because the observers move relative to each other.
boundary_test.confirms: The trigger is observer acceleration, not observer motion in general.

teaching_routes.title: Reveal Newton/FBD conceptual spine
entry_needs: Velocity-versus-acceleration distinction from the kinematics prerequisite.
learner_actions: Keep individual forces distinct from their net result.
Assign forces to one chosen body.
Declare observer acceleration before using a pseudo-force convention.
help_plan: Use a released low-friction cart for the first-law contrast.
Use two separate body inventories before any force equations.
Use roadside versus accelerating-bus descriptions for the observer boundary.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: Completed conceptual constructions are visible; no quantitative force relation is introduced.

source_preferences.reason: The four rungs are authored here without promoting candidate-packet authority.

when_not_suitable: Do not treat the absence of a FREE_BODY_DIAGRAM representation record as permission to invent one.
Do not turn these distinctions into a quantitative force-law lesson.

teaching_routes.title: Elicit Newton/FBD conceptual spine
entry_needs: Same intrinsic coverage as Core1A; no inferred learner mastery.
learner_actions: Commit to motion and force predictions before reveal.
help_plan: Ask which body receives each force before naming any pairing rule.
Ask whether a physical agent changed before introducing a pseudo-force.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: Prediction, reconstruction, misconception diagnosis and boundary tests precede the closed reveal.

source_preferences.reason: Each elicitation cycle is authored specifically for the corresponding rung.

when_not_suitable: Do not substitute a declarative diagram for the learner's body-ownership decision.

data.meaning: Illustrative steady speed available to compiled study obligations; none of the authored exits depends on its numerical value.
data.locator: Author-created illustrative value; no measurement or curriculum provenance claimed.
